title: Dyna Z12 floors and sills: assessing corrosion before restoration
author: Caramagnols
excerpt: Flat floor, crossmembers, sills, mountings and old welds determine the size of the project. An ordered inspection separates local damage from a weakened structure.
content:
A freshly painted Dyna Z12 can conceal a major project; a dull car may retain a sound, understandable base. The difference rarely sits on the bonnet. It appears in floors, sills, crossmembers, suspension mountings and the repairs accumulated beneath trim.

Construction identifies the critical areas

Dyna Z was designed around a broad flat floor connected laterally by its sills. Two tubular crossmembers pass beneath the benches; a third at the front carries the engine, gearbox and front suspension assembly, attached by bolts. The rear suspension is secured to the rear crossmember. The outer envelope provides aerodynamic form and protection, while this base carries much of the load.

Type Z12 replaced the extensive Duralinox content of early Z1 with an all-steel body. Club figures show weight rising from about 710 to 875 kg between those phases. This industrial change does not make every Dyna Z a rusted wreck, but preservation and repair quality become central when choosing a project.

Before lifting the car

A distorted lifting area, swollen sill or cracking panel rules out improvisation with a jack. The owner should indicate the supports normally used. On an unknown car, a professional with a lift and experience of old vehicles can choose areas capable of carrying the load. Going beneath a vehicle held only by its original jack is never an inspection method.

Start at ground level with a lamp: unequal height, a wheel poorly centred in its opening, a dropping door, irregular gap or distorted roof. No one sign condemns the shell. Their accumulation points towards diagonal measurement and a geometry check before dismantling.

The floor from inside the cabin

Carpets, insulation and benches may trap moisture. Removing them with the owner’s agreement exposes pressings, joints and repairs. Firm surface pitting presents a different problem from perforation around a mounting. Plates laid over the old floor may feel solid while corrosion continues between two layers.

Footwells are not the only areas. Returns against the sills, control apertures, seat bases and crossmember edges need close photographs. After gentle cleaning, colour differences between original metal, welds and added panels often establish the order of previous work.

Sills and door pillars

Sills connect the sides of the floor. Their condition appears in aperture shape, door alignment and continuity of joints. On Z12, front doors open rearwards and load the centre pillar through their hinges. A door that drops can result from worn pins, but also from weakened mountings or surrounding metal.

Observe both sides symmetrically. A change of profile, thick filler, blocked drains or an irregular line of welds marks an intervention worth documenting. A magnet and paint-thickness gauge can add evidence on accessible surfaces without replacing internal examination of closed sections.

Crossmembers and suspension mountings

Around crossmembers, corrosion becomes a matter of position and spread. Perforation away from a loaded point differs from a crack or thinning beside a mounting. Front assembly, powertrain and rear suspension transmit forces through these structures; repair must restore shape, thickness and continuity rather than merely cover a hole.

Photograph bolts, plates, welds and panel edges before stripping. A new fastener in old surroundings may show normal maintenance or more extensive repair. History, invoices and work photographs can separate those possibilities.

Boot, wheel housings and body ends

Empty the boot. Spare-wheel space, corners, wheel-housing joints and lamp areas collect dirt or damp. At the front, the large bonnet opening aids access, though thrown oil and old leaks may conceal panel boundaries.

Outer panels also reveal impacts. An interrupted moulding line, left-right differences or a panel held under tension by repair can lead towards deeper damage. Conversely, a dented non-structural panel does not justify declaring the shell beyond use.

Recognising a usable old repair

An old weld is not automatically poor. Documented work made on sound metal and protected on both faces may be preferable to a never-opened but deeply corroded area. Geometry, edge preparation, continuity, absence of trapped rust and a clear account of replaced metal are the useful criteria.

Stacked sheets, broken welds on thinning metal, filler acting as structure and sealed cavities without protection need further work. Cost then comes less from the visible area than from dismantling required to reach sound material.

Build a survey before asking for a quotation

AreaFindingNext step
Main floorPitting, holes, added platesClean, test and establish true extent
Sills and aperturesDistortion, filler, door gapsInternal inspection and geometry
CrossmembersThinning, crack, previous weldsEvaluation by a body specialist familiar with the structure
MountingsCorrosion close to fastenersNo road use before an approved repair
Boot and housingsDamp, impact, open jointsLocal dismantling and protection after repair

The survey distinguishes visible faults, areas still to open and points already measured. A credible quotation includes a margin for hidden damage. It also names parts to preserve, especially when repair might destroy evidence used to identify the model year.

Local repair or an overall rebuild

A few confined defects on a stable structure allow work by area. Continuous damage between floors, sills and mountings requires an overall strategy that holds geometry during cutting. Complete dismantling is not proof of quality in itself; it becomes appropriate when access, protection and structural continuity demand it.

The purchase then depends on a combination of price, trim completeness, mechanical condition, available skills and intended result. A heavily corroded Z12 can be saved, but its budget cannot be based on a car needing only local floor repairs.
